items.readable_text:
Content:
Remember that longer sides in a triangle are opposite to larger angles, and vice versa. But what if two (or more) sides have the same length?

Content:
As you might have guessed, if two sides have the same length, then the opposite angles have the same measure. And vice-versa: if two angles have the same measure, then the opposite sides have the same length.

Content:
So, we obtain the following important properties of isosceles and equilateral triangles:

Content:
- A triangle is equilateral if and only if all of its angles are of [MATH: 60^\circ.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3ff8fa10e5b43b23287dfb0fba9ac84d]

Content:
- A triangle is isosceles if and only if it has two congruent angles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/80c70e314a4259ba9e4e4a1ab0d997d5]

Content:
Note: The statement above encompasses two theorems:

Content:
- The isosceles triangle theorem:

> If a triangle is isosceles, then the base angles are congruent.
- The converse isosceles triangle theorem:

> If two angles in a triangle have the same measure, then the triangle must be isosceles.

items.title: Calculating the Measure of an Angle Using the Isosceles Triangle Theorem

sections.normalized_html: What is the measure of [MATH: \angle{A}] in the triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] below?
sections.readable_text:
What is the measure of [MATH: \angle{A}] in the triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] below?

[IMG: /graphics/177f2f9a960df0322f5a7d66640162c3]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since two sides are congruent, [MATH: \overline{BC} \cong \overline{AB},] we conclude that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is isosceles. Consequently, the base angles must have the same measure:

[MATH: m\angle C = m\angle A = x -10^\circ]

Now, since the internal angles of any triangle sum to [MATH: 180^\circ,] we have [MATH: m∠A + m∠B + m∠C|= 180^{∘}; (x − 10^{∘}) + (x + 20^{∘}) + (x − 10^{∘})|= 180^{∘}; 3x|= 180^{∘}; x|= 60^{∘}.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: x=60^\circ] into the equation for the measure of [MATH: \angle A] gives [MATH: m∠A|= x − 10^{∘}; = 60^{∘} − 10^{∘}; = 50^{∘}.]

So [MATH: m\angle A = 50^\circ.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Remember that longer sides in a triangle are opposite to larger angles, and vice versa. But what if two (or more) sides have the same length?

Content:
As you might have guessed, if two sides have the same length, then the opposite angles have the same measure. And vice-versa: if two angles have the same measure, then the opposite sides have the same length.

Content:
So, we obtain the following important properties of isosceles and equilateral triangles:

Content:
- A triangle is equilateral if and only if all of its angles are of [MATH: 60^\circ.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3ff8fa10e5b43b23287dfb0fba9ac84d]

Content:
- A triangle is isosceles if and only if it has two congruent angles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/80c70e314a4259ba9e4e4a1ab0d997d5]

Content:
Note: The statement above encompasses two theorems:

Content:
- The isosceles triangle theorem:

> If a triangle is isosceles, then the base angles are congruent.
- The converse isosceles triangle theorem:

> If two angles in a triangle have the same measure, then the triangle must be isosceles.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Measure of an Angle Using the Isosceles Triangle Theorem

Example Prompt:
What is the measure of [MATH: \angle{A}] in the triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] below?

[IMG: /graphics/177f2f9a960df0322f5a7d66640162c3]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since two sides are congruent, [MATH: \overline{BC} \cong \overline{AB},] we conclude that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is isosceles. Consequently, the base angles must have the same measure:

[MATH: m\angle C = m\angle A = x -10^\circ]

Now, since the internal angles of any triangle sum to [MATH: 180^\circ,] we have
[MATH: m∠A + m∠B + m∠C|= 180^{∘}; (x − 10^{∘}) + (x + 20^{∘}) + (x − 10^{∘})|= 180^{∘}; 3x|= 180^{∘}; x|= 60^{∘}.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: x=60^\circ] into the equation for the measure of [MATH: \angle A] gives
[MATH: m∠A|= x − 10^{∘}; = 60^{∘} − 10^{∘}; = 50^{∘}.]

So [MATH: m\angle A = 50^\circ.]

We conclude that [MATH: AB=6.]

Item 11 — Example: Finding the Measure of an Angle Given Multiple Triangles

Example Prompt:
In the figure below, [MATH: m\angle{CAD}=100^\circ.] What is the measure of [MATH: \angle{D}?]

[IMG: /graphics/934feef3e7eec5a8ba0ed5b6601f1fe1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] is an equilateral triangle. Consequently, all of the interior angles must be equal to [MATH: 60^\circ\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: m\angle{BAC}=m\angle{ABC}=m\angle{C}=60^\circ]

Also, since [MATH: \triangle{ADB}] is an isosceles triangle, the base angles must have equal measure:

[MATH: m\angle{BAD}=m\angle{ABD}]

[IMG: /graphics/ab0b53efa7aa0662bcb9570f9fbc80ed]

Now, since we're told that [MATH: m\angle{CAD}=100^\circ,] we have
[MATH: m∠BAD|= m∠CAD − m∠BAC; = 100^{∘} − 60^{∘}; = 40^{∘}.]

Finally, in [MATH: \triangle{BAD}], we have
[MATH: m∠BAD + m∠D + m∠ABD|= 180^{∘}; 2m∠BAD + m∠D|= 180^{∘}; 2 ⋅ 40^{∘} + m∠D|= 180^{∘}; 80^{∘} + m∠D|= 180^{∘}; m∠D|= 100^{∘}.]
